newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers pull back tractors, end protest.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers pull back tractors, end protest.

text.p: Greek farmers pulled back their tractors from major roads on Sunday but warned the government they would resume their protests if their demands for cheaper fuel and state subsidies were not met.
"I am bitter because we came out empty handed," said cotton grower Costas Papadimitriou. "But we will return for a third round to push for our just demands."
The farmers, who blocked national roads for 25 days in December, began a new protest last week and on Thursday lined the main north-south highway with some 2,000 tractors, threatening to block it.
They eluded police a number of times, driving their tractors through vast cotton fields and across rivers to reach key points of the national highway.
Police eventually managed to immobilise the tractors on Friday deflating their tyres.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, facing critisism for doing nothing to prevent the December blockade, sent 5,000 police to central Greece with strict orders to keep roads open.

The farmers accused police of damaging the tractors, despite a denial by the government, and a crowd of 5,000 gathered outside the central village of Almyros on Sunday before heading to the highway to continue repairs.

"They pulled off the radio from the dashboard. They cut electrical cables and threw sugar in the petrol tank to destroy the engine. They then slashed two tyres with knives," said onion grower Antonis Anagnostopoulos.
Other farmers showed reporters smashed windshields, headlights and cut ventilator belts.
Their retreat from the highways was seen as a second victory for Simitis who turned down repeated requests by the farmers to meet him.

Simitis, determined to push through his tough economic policies, sent five of his top ministers on a tour of central Greece on Saturday to meet residents and explain the government's policy on farming.

He has said the farmers' demands could not be met as they violated. the European Union common agriculture policy, adding that there was no money in the budget for special interest groups like the farmers.
The government hopes the protests will ease as farmers will have to return to their fields in two weeks for seasonal work.
The farmers are among a number of groups protesting or striking against a 1997 budget described as the toughest in 15 years, and against strict incomes and tax policies.
Teachers have been on strike for a month while labour confederations have staged repeated walkouts against the government. Protest rallies clog traffic almost daily in the Greek capital.
